items.context: The description suggests optionally doing a lightweight health check (e.g., GET /api/tags) to confirm Ollama is reachable, not just configured. This adds latency to the options endpoint but provides more accurate status. The config-presence check alone can't detect Ollama being down or unreachable.

options.label: Config presence only (no health check)
options.rationale: Simplest fix. Returns available: true if OllamaURL is set. Zero added latency. Matches the pattern aiChain() already uses. If Ollama is down, the error surfaces at generation time instead. Recommended because this is the minimal fix that solves the stated problem — users see 'configured' vs 'not configured' accurately.

options.label: Config presence + async health check with 2s timeout
options.rationale: More accurate — distinguishes 'configured but unreachable' from 'configured and ready'. Adds up to 2s latency on the options endpoint. Could use a goroutine to check Ollama and OpenRouter in parallel. Complexity is moderate.

options.label: Config presence + cached health check (background refresh)
options.rationale: Best UX — zero latency on the endpoint, but requires a background goroutine that periodically pings providers and caches the result. More infrastructure (cache, ticker, shutdown). Overkill for an S-effort fix.

items.context: OpenRouter is a cloud API keyed by OPENROUTER_API_KEY. Unlike Ollama (local service), we can't easily health-check it without making an API call that might have rate-limit or cost implications. The question is whether config presence is sufficient or if we should validate the key.

options.label: Config presence only (key is non-empty)
options.rationale: Consistent with Ollama approach. If the key is set, report available. Invalid keys will error at generation time. This is the standard pattern — most APIs don't pre-validate keys on a status endpoint.

options.label: Validate key format (starts with 'sk-or-')
options.rationale: Slightly more helpful — catches obvious misconfigurations like setting the wrong env var. But key format may change and this creates a brittle check.

items.context: The existing test uses setupMockServerWithConfig(t, cfg) which creates a full test server with a router. We need to test 4 config permutations (neither, Ollama only, OpenRouter only, both). We can either write 4 separate test functions or use table-driven tests.

options.label: Table-driven test with 4 subtests
options.rationale: Idiomatic Go pattern. Single TestGenerateOptions_Availability function with t.Run() subtests. Less boilerplate, easier to add cases later. Recommended because it's the standard Go testing pattern for permutation testing.

options.label: 4 separate test functions
options.rationale: Each test is self-contained and independently named. More verbose but each failure is immediately identifiable by function name. Better if the setup differs significantly between cases (it doesn't here).

items.text: The frontend (generate-options.tsx) already handles dynamic availability correctly — it renders a green checkmark for available: true and a red X with 'Not configured' for available: false. No UI changes are needed.

The existing TestGenerateOptions test (scanner_plugin_test.go L295+) only validates response structure (status 200, has providers array, has elements array). It uses config.Default() which has empty OllamaURL and OpenRouterAPIKey, so both providers should show available: false. This test can remain as-is; new tests will cover the availability permutations.

plan_updates: Created initial plan.md with all 13 sections. Problem clarity and scope are well-defined from the spec. Implementation strategy covers the handler fix and test expansion. Testing plan includes a 4-case permutation matrix. Two open decisions remain: health check strategy and test structure approach.
